name: Tetrapeptide-5

card.summary: A short cosmetic peptide in eye creams that people use to make puffy under-eyes look smoother and less swollen.

quick.overview:
Tetrapeptide-5 is a four-amino-acid peptide added to eye creams and gels. People use it to reduce the look of puffy eyelids and under-eye bags.

It is found in over-the-counter products and is often combined with other eye-area ingredients.
quick.mechanism: Ingredient makers describe it as acting on swelling-related pathways and glycation in the thin skin around the eyes. A 2021 cell study measured its activity on angiotensin-converting enzyme 1 [1].
quick.risks: It is a topical cosmetic ingredient with a low reported irritation profile in leave-on eye products. Labels advise stopping use if irritation develops.

lead: Tetrapeptide-5, listed on labels as acetyl tetrapeptide-5, is a short four-amino-acid peptide used in eye creams and gels aimed at puffy eyelids and under-eye bags. People apply it to make the eye area look smoother, less swollen and more rested [1]. It is sold under the trade name Eyeseryl and is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug [1].

The ingredient is described by its supplier as working through anti-edema and anti-glycation effects [1]. A 2021 laboratory study of five cosmetic peptides on skin cells found acetyl tetrapeptide-5 at 100 micrograms per milliliter was the optimal concentration for activity on angiotensin-converting enzyme 1, one of the measures the researchers used to design anti-aging and protective formulas [2].

The manufacturer reports an in-vivo study in 20 volunteers using a 10% solution of the ingredient (about 0.01% pure peptide), with 70% showing improvement in puffiness by day 15 and 95% by day 60 [1]. This is manufacturer-supplied data; no independent trial of the peptide in the eye area was located.

chain: Applied to the eyelid and under-eye skin in a cream or gel
Peptide described as acting on fluid and glycation-related pathways
Eye area looks less puffy and smoother
angle.text: Tetrapeptide-5 is applied in eye products to reduce the look of morning puffiness and bags, usually as part of an eye-care routine with other ingredients such as caffeine. Its supplier reports improvement in puffiness in volunteers [1].

infobox: Cosmetic ingredient; listed as a humectant in CosIng [1]

paras: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 appears in eye gels and creams marketed for puffiness and a tired look. It is often paired with other eye-area actives in the same formula [1].

Suppliers describe the peptide as reducing swelling and glycation in the tissue around the eye [1]. The 2021 cell study measured activity on angiotensin-converting enzyme 1, hydroxyproline content and other markers across five cosmetic peptides in human skin fibroblasts under oxidative stress [2]. An ingredient guide notes that puffiness has several causes and that water accumulation is the situation where a topical anti-edema ingredient is most plausibly relevant, whereas fat accumulation with age is a different cause [1].

In the manufacturer's study of 20 volunteers using a cream with 10% Eyeseryl, the share showing improvement in puffiness rose from 70% at day 15 to 95% at day 60, with roughly a third each showing slight, moderate and good improvement [1].
As a topical cosmetic ingredient it is used in leave-on eye products at low concentrations; product labels advise avoiding contact with the inside of the eye and stopping use if irritation occurs.
No independent human trials found. Laboratory work on skin cells has tested the peptide alone and in cosmetic peptide mixtures [2], and the manufacturer reports a 20-volunteer in-vivo study [1].
